title: Experience shows pagans capable of civil righteousness
source_text: V. Et certe ipsa experientia planum est hominem etiam Ethnicum & nulla salutari Dei cognitione imbutum, posse depositum & mutuum reddere, cognatos colere, parentes honorare, Eleemosynam pauperibus largiri, temperanter & sobrie vivere, & plura ejusmodi: & sic multa facere apud homines, quos interiora latent, speciosa & laudabilia: & ex quibus exurgit justitia quaedam & honestas civilis: qualis fuit in Socrate, Epaminonda, Phocione, Scipione, Catone, & pluribus apud Gentiles laudatis viris, quorum exempla plerisque Christianis pudorem suffundere debent.
pass_a_gloss: V. And certainly by experience itself it is plain that man even a Heathen and imbued with no saving knowledge of God, can return a deposit and a loan, cherish kinsfolk, honour parents, bestow Alms on the poor, live temperately and soberly, and more things of the kind: and so do many things before men, from whom inward things lie hidden, specious and laudable: and from which there arises a certain righteousness and civil honesty: such as was in Socrates, Epaminondas, Phocion, Scipio, Cato, and many men praised among the Gentiles, whose examples ought to bring a blush of shame on most Christians.
pass_b_english: Thesis V. Experience itself makes it plain that a man, even a pagan with no saving knowledge of God, can repay a deposit or a loan, care for his relatives, honour his parents, give alms to the poor, live temperately and soberly, and do many other such things.

In this way he can do many things that look fine and praiseworthy before men, who cannot see what lies within, and from them arises a kind of righteousness and civil uprightness. Such was found in Socrates, Epaminondas, Phocion, Scipio, Cato and many other men praised among the Gentiles, whose examples ought to make most Christians blush.

lemmas.gloss: imbued with no saving knowledge of God
before men, from whom inward things lie hidden
a certain righteousness and civil honesty
ought to bring a blush of shame on most Christians

choices.why: Melanchthon's term (Apology, art. 18) for the outward uprightness of which reason is capable; 'righteousness' keeps the link with justitia elsewhere in the treatise.
